01.note: Ulla came to visit Rav Yehuda on a Festival, and Ulla's servant tilted the oil lamp so that the oil would run away from the wick and the light would go out sooner. Rav Yehuda challenged Ulla with a teaching that anyone who takes oil from a burning lamp is guilty of extinguishing it. Ulla agreed and answered that his servant had done it without his knowledge.
01.why: The Gemara is discussing the mishna's rule that a fallen candelabrum may not be set up on a Festival; this lamp incident opens a series of rulings on what counts as putting out a light on a Festival.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage visiting Rav Yehuda's house; his servant tilted the lamp.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The host, who objects that tilting the lamp is a form of extinguishing.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot. Most work forbidden on Shabbat is forbidden on these days too, except work needed to prepare food.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core legal code the Talmud discusses.
Putting out a fire is one of the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat; the teaching says even making a lamp burn out sooner counts as doing it.

02.note: A teaching reports that the house of Rabban Gamliel swept the dining room and put incense on coals on a Festival, though others did not. Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok said he had often gone with his father into Rabban Gamliel's house and seen how it was really done. The room was swept the day before and covered with sheets, and the sheets were lifted when the guests arrived, so the house was found clean on its own. In the same way, iron coal pans were filled with fragrant smoke the day before and plugged, then opened when the guests came, so the house was perfumed on its own. The other Sages answered that if so, this would be allowed even on Shabbat.
02.why: Rav Asi had said the dispute over incense was only about perfuming clothes; the Gemara cites this account to challenge him, since the Sages' reply implies even incense for its smell is forbidden, and it then reverses his statement.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader whose household practices on the Festival are described.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
people.about: Eyewitness who often went with his father into Rabban Gamliel's house.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's father, whom he followed into Rabban Gamliel's house.

terms.meaning: A collection of early rabbinic teachings arranged alongside the Mishna, the core legal code the Talmud discusses.
The dining room, where people reclined on couches to eat.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which most work is forbidden except work needed to prepare food.

03.note: Rabbi Yosei reports that Theodosius of Rome, a leader of the Jews there, set up a custom for the Roman Jews to eat a whole roasted kid goat on the night of Passover, as was done with the Passover offering in the Temple. The Sages sent him a message: were you not Theodosius, we would have decreed ostracism on you, because you are feeding the Jewish people consecrated food outside the Temple.
03.why: The mishna lists preparing a whole kid on Passover night as one of Rabban Gamliel's leniencies, which the Rabbis forbid; this report shows the Sages' objection, and the Gemara then explains they meant the meat only looked like a Temple offering.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Theodosius of Rome
people.about: Leader of the Jewish community in Rome who started the custom.

terms.meaning: A young goat roasted whole, with its innards placed over its head, the way the Passover lamb was roasted in the Temple.
A formal ban by the Sages that cut a person off from normal dealings with the community.
Meat of offerings dedicated to the Temple, which may be eaten only in and around the Temple itself.

04.note: Rav Nahman asked Hama bar Adda, a messenger who traveled between Babylonia and the Land of Israel, to go out of his way to the Ladder of Tyre and ask Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi what the rule was for being carried in a chair on a Festival. By the time he got there, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had died. Instead he found Rabbi Zerika, who told him that Rabbi Ami allowed it, provided the person is not carried on the shoulders. Rav Yosef, son of Rabba, explained that this means on poles resting on the bearers' shoulders.
04.why: A teaching forbids going out in a carried chair on a Festival, yet Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported that it was allowed for a man the public needed; Rav Nahman wanted the rule from him directly.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage in Babylonia who sends the question.

people.name: Hama bar Adda
people.about: Messenger of the academies who carried the question to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: Sage in Tyre to whom the question was addressed; he died before it reached him.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Sage who answered instead, quoting Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rabba
people.about: Sage who explained what 'not carried on the shoulders' means.

terms.meaning: A steep coastal pass near the city of Tyre, on a roundabout route into the Land of Israel.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which ordinary weekday activity is restricted.
A seat carried by bearers, like a litter; using one looked like a weekday activity.

05.note: A man in Babylonia, whose name is not given, wished that he might go up to the Land of Israel and hear a ruling from the mouth of the Sage who taught it. When he got there he found Rabbi Zeira and asked him whether he had really said that the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Zeira said no: what he had said was only that it stands to reason.
05.why: The Gemara is debating whether a firstborn animal's blemish may be examined on a Festival; Rabbi Abba had claimed Rabbi Zeira ruled like Rabbi Shimon, and this trip checks that report at its source.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Sage in the Land of Israel whose reported ruling the traveler came to check.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Earlier Sage whose opinion on the question was said to be the law.

terms.meaning: Rabbi Zeira's way of saying his view was his own reasoning, not a received tradition that the law is so.

06.note: Ami of Vardina examined firstborn animals for the household of the Nasi, but on Festivals he would not examine them. When Rabbi Ami was told, he said Ami did well. The Gemara objects that Rabbi Ami himself examined firstborns, and answers that he looked at the blemish the day before and on the Festival only asked how it happened. So it was with Rava: a man brought him a firstborn near nightfall on the eve of a Festival while Rava was washing his hair. Rava looked up, saw the blemish, and told him to come back tomorrow. The next day Rava asked how it happened; the owner said barley lay on the far side of a thorn fence and the animal cut its lip reaching for it. Rava asked if he had caused it, and he said no. The text does not say what Rava then ruled.
06.why: The Gemara has been discussing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda over examining firstborn blemishes on a Festival; right after, it explains why Rava asked whether the owner caused the blemish, since causing one is forbidden.

people.name: Ami of Vardina
people.about: Examiner of firstborn animals for the household of the Nasi, who would not examine them on Festivals.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who approved of Ami of Vardina's practice.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage before whom a firstborn was brought on the eve of a Festival.

terms.meaning: A male firstborn calf, lamb or kid belonged to a priest as an offering. If it had a permanent blemish, an expert could declare it fit to be slaughtered and eaten as ordinary meat.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot.

07.note: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, used to divide meat between them on a Festival by weighing one portion against the other on a scale. The text tells nothing more of the incident.
07.why: The mishna forbids weighing meat on a Festival, with Rabbi Yehuda allowing it only against a vessel or cleaver; the Gemara asks whose view these two followed, and answers that it was Rabbi Yehoshua, who allows weighing portion against portion.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Sage who divided meat with Rabbi Shimon on a Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who shared the meat with Rabbi Hiyya.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which weekday business practices like weighing goods are restricted.

07.flag: Only one sentence of event (two Sages weighing meat); the rest of the story segment is the Gemara's legal question about it.

08.note: Rav Nehemya, son of Rav Yosef, recalled standing before Rava on a Festival while Rava ran a knife over the rim of a basket. He asked whether Rava was sharpening it or cleaning off the fat. Rava said he was removing the fat, but Rav Nehemya could tell he was really sharpening it. He held that sharpening was allowed, but that this should not be taught as a public ruling.
08.why: Shmuel taught that a knife may be run over another only to clean it, not to sharpen it, while Rava had just credited Rav Hisda with ruling like Rabbi Yehuda, who allows tasks that make food preparation possible; this shows Rava following that ruling quietly.

people.name: Rav Nehemya, son of Rav Yosef
people.about: Student who watched Rava and tells the story.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who ran a knife over a basket rim on a Festival.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which work is restricted except what is needed to prepare food.

terms.term: the halakha, but a ruling is not issued
terms.meaning: A rule that is correct in law but that Sages would not announce publicly, so that people would not take it too far.

09.note: Abaye recalled standing before his teacher Rabba on a Festival while Rabba ran a knife over the edge of a millstone. Abaye asked whether he meant to sharpen it or to clean off the fat. Rabba said to remove the fat, but Abaye could tell he was sharpening it. Rabba held that sharpening was allowed, but that this should not be taught as a public ruling.
09.why: This follows Rav Nehemya's almost identical account of Rava; the two reports together show leading Sages quietly following Rabbi Yehuda's lenient view on sharpening a knife on a Festival.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Student who watched his teacher and tells the story.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Abaye's master and teacher, who ran a knife over a millstone on a Festival.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which work is restricted except what is needed to prepare food.

terms.term: the halakha, but a ruling is not issued
terms.meaning: A rule that is correct in law but that Sages would not announce publicly, so that people would not take it too far.

10.note: Abba Shaul ben Botnit, a Sage who was also a grocer, would fill his measures on the eve of a Festival and hand them to customers on the Festival; he did the same on the intermediate days so as not to lose time in the study hall. He gathered three hundred jugs of wine from the foam of his measures, which he felt he had not earned, and his colleagues gathered three hundred jugs of oil from what was left in their measures. They brought them to the Temple treasurers in Jerusalem, who said they need not do this. They said they did not want it. The treasurers told them to use it for communal needs, which Rav Hisda explains as cisterns, ditches and caves for water.
10.why: The mishna on measuring goods for a Festival cites Abba Shaul's practice, and the Gemara has just explained how Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis treat filling a measuring vessel; the baraita adds more about the man and his scruples.

people.name: Abba Shaul ben Botnit
people.about: A Sage and grocer, careful not to profit from anything that was not his.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage who explains what 'communal needs' means.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is permitted but the days are still part of the holiday.
Officials in Jerusalem who received and managed funds and goods given to the Temple.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core legal code the Talmud discusses.
Public works for everyone's benefit, used to repay a theft when the victims cannot be identified.

11.note: Rav Yosef's wife was sifting flour on the back side of a sieve. He told her: look, I want good bread, a hint that she could sift in the normal way. Rav Ashi's wife was sifting flour onto a table. Rav Ashi said that his wife was the daughter of Rami bar Hama, a man careful in his deeds, and she would not do this had she not seen it in her father's house.
11.why: The Gemara is debating whether flour may be sifted a second time on a Festival; Rav Nahman has said every woman in Neharde'a already does it, and these two households show how it was done in practice.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who tells his wife she may sift flour normally.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who trusts his wife's practice, learned in her father's house.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: Rav Ashi's father-in-law, called a master of good deeds.

terms.meaning: Sifting with the sieve upside down, an unusual way of doing it that marks the work as different from an ordinary weekday.

12.note: Rav Natan bar Abba, quoting Rav, said the wealthy Jews of Babylonia will go down to Gehenna. He illustrates it with Shabbetai bar Marinus, who came to Babylonia and asked the wealthy there to invest with him in a business venture; they refused. He asked them for food to live on, and they refused that too. He said they must descend from the mixed multitude, because anyone who has compassion for others is known to be a descendant of Abraham, and anyone who does not, is not.
12.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Natan bar Abba on trimming a lamp wick, and so gathers his other teachings together to make them easier to remember; this is one of them.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Abba
people.about: Sage who reports Rav's saying about the wealthy of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose harsh saying about the wealthy is quoted.

people.name: Shabbetai bar Marinus
people.about: A visitor to Babylonia refused both an investment and food by the wealthy there.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment for the wicked after death.
The non-Israelites who left Egypt with the Israelites in the Exodus, not descendants of Abraham.
A partnership in which an investor lends money and shares the profits.

13.note: Abaye's millhouse sprang a leak on Shabbat, and he came to his teacher Rabba for advice. Rabba told him to bring his bed into the millhouse, so the dirty water would count like a container of excrement in his living space, which may be carried out, and then to remove it. Abaye sat and puzzled over whether one may create such a situation on purpose. Meanwhile his millhouse collapsed. Abaye said: I had this coming for going against my master.
13.why: A teaching has just allowed a vessel placed under a leak on Shabbat to be emptied and put back again; this case asks what one may do when that is not enough to handle the water.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Owner of the leaking millhouse, and Rabba's student.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who tells him how to get rid of the water.

terms.meaning: Something so repulsive that, although normally it may not be moved on Shabbat, the Sages let a person carry it out of the room where he is.
Items that may not be moved or handled on Shabbat because they are not meant for use that day.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest on which many kinds of work are forbidden.

14.note: When Rabbi Abba went up from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he prayed that he would say something there that would be accepted. He found a group of leading Sages asking why the water and salt a woman borrows are not simply absorbed into her dough. Rabbi Abba said: if a man's one measure of wheat got mixed into another's ten, would the other man just eat it all and be glad? They laughed at him. He said: did I take your cloaks, that you laugh at me? They laughed at him again.
14.why: The mishna rules that a dough made with a neighbor's water and salt may be carried on a Festival only where both women may walk; the Sages asked why those small ingredients still count, and afterward Rabbi Oshaya says they were right to laugh while Rav Safra defends Rabbi Abba.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Sage newly arrived from Babylonia who hoped his words would be accepted.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: One of the Sages he found discussing the mishna (in one version).

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: One of the Sages he found discussing the mishna (in one version).

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: One of the Sages he found discussing the mishna (in one version).

terms.meaning: On a Festival an object may be carried only as far as its owner may walk; an item belonging to two people is limited by both.
When a small amount of something is mixed into a much larger amount, the law can treat the small part as if it has disappeared into the larger.
A measure of volume for grain and other dry goods.

15.note: Rav Hana bar Hanilai hung meat on the bar of his host's door while away from his own town on a Festival, and then asked whether he could take it home. He came before Rav Huna, who told him: if you hung it yourself, go and take it; if they hung it for you, do not take it.
15.why: Rav holds that an item left in someone's house follows the keeper's travel limits unless a corner was set aside for the owner; the Gemara asks how Rav Huna, Rav's student, could rule this way, and answers that a door bar counts as such a corner.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Hanilai
people.about: Sage who hung his meat at his host's house and asked whether he could take it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage who gave him the ruling.

terms.meaning: Here, a legal device that lets a person walk beyond the usual limit outside his town on Shabbat or a Festival.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which there are limits on how far a person and his belongings may travel.

16.note: Rav Nahman and Rabbi Yitzhak were eating a meal together, and Rav Nahman asked for a teaching. Rabbi Yitzhak quoted Rabbi Yohanan: one may not talk during a meal, for fear of choking. After they ate, he quoted Rabbi Yohanan again: our patriarch Jacob did not die. Rav Nahman asked whether he had been eulogized, embalmed and buried for nothing; Rabbi Yitzhak said he was drawing it from a verse that links Jacob to his living descendants. Rabbi Yitzhak also said anyone who says 'Rahab, Rahab' at once has a seminal emission; when Rav Nahman said it did not affect him, Rabbi Yitzhak said he meant men who knew her. As they parted, Rav Nahman asked for a blessing, and Rabbi Yitzhak began a parable about a hungry, thirsty traveler who found a tree with sweet fruit, shade and a stream beneath it.
16.why: The Gemara has been reporting questions Rav Nahman put to Rabbi Yitzhak about Samuel and Saul; this meal continues their conversation.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who eats with Rabbi Yitzhak and asks him for teachings and a blessing.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: Sage who shares teachings at the meal and answers with a parable.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage whose teachings Rabbi Yitzhak quotes.

terms.meaning: The woman of Jericho in the Book of Joshua; here she is noted for her great beauty.
A short illustrative story used to make a point.

16.flag: The story stops partway through the tree parable; its ending and the blessing itself fall in the segments marked AFTER.

17.note: The emperor's daughter said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, an ugly man: woe to glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel. He asked whether her father kept his wine in simple clay vessels. When she asked what else he should use, he said that people as important as they should use gold and silver. She told her father, who moved his wine into gold and silver vessels, and it went sour. When the emperor learned that the advice came from Rabbi Yehoshua, he summoned him and asked why. Rabbi Yehoshua said he had answered her the way she had spoken to him. The emperor objected that there are handsome people who are learned; Rabbi Yehoshua replied that had they been ugly, they would have been even more learned.
17.why: Rabbi Oshaya has just taught that Torah is like water, wine and milk, kept only in the plainest vessels, so it stays only with the humble; this exchange illustrates his point.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage described as an ugly man, mocked by the emperor's daughter.

people.name: the daughter of the emperor
people.about: The Roman emperor's daughter, who mocks the Sage's looks.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler whose wine turns sour on the Sage's advice.

18.note: Rabbi Yohanan met the young son of Reish Lakish and asked him to recite the verse he had learned that day: 'A tithe shall you tithe.' Asked what it meant, Rabbi Yohanan said: give a tithe so that you will become wealthy. The boy asked how he knew, and Rabbi Yohanan said: go and test it. The boy objected that the Torah says 'You shall not test the Lord your God.' Rabbi Yohanan answered, quoting Rabbi Hoshaya, that testing God is forbidden except in this case, as the prophet Malachi says of tithes, 'test Me now by this.'
18.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yohanan's own reading of 'a tithe shall you tithe' as 'tithe so you will become wealthy'; this exchange shows him defending it to a sharp child.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who questions the boy and explains the verse.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage whose young son Rabbi Yohanan meets.

people.name: Rabbi Hoshaya
people.about: Sage whose teaching Rabbi Yohanan quotes.

terms.meaning: A tenth of one's produce, which the Torah requires be set aside and given away.

19.note: Three Sages, Rav Huna bar Manoah, Rav Shmuel bar Idi and Rav Hiyya from Vastanya, were regular students of Rava. When Rava died they came to study with Rav Pappa, but whenever he taught a ruling that did not seem reasonable to them, they signaled to one another, and Rav Pappa was hurt. In a dream the verse was read to him: 'And I cut off the three shepherds in one month.' The next day, as they took their leave, he said to them: may the Rabbis go in peace. The text does not say what became of them.
19.why: The Gemara has just discussed the same verse from Zechariah about three shepherds cut off in one month, applied to Moses, Aaron and Miriam; this story is told because Rav Pappa dreamed of that verse.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Manoah
people.about: One of three students who came to Rav Pappa after Rava died.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Idi
people.about: One of the three students.

people.name: Rav Hiyya from Vastanya
people.about: One of the three students.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The teacher of the three, whose death sends them to Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Their new teacher, offended by their gestures.

terms.meaning: A parting phrase; the translation explains that Rav Pappa took it to mean this was their final farewell.

20.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi studied regularly with Rav Pappa and raised many objections to his teachings. One day he saw Rav Pappa fall on his face in prayer and heard him say: may the Merciful One save me from the shame of Shimi. Rav Shimi resolved to be silent and raised no more objections.
20.why: It follows the story of Rav Pappa's three students, who also hurt him by doubting his teaching, as a second case of the same kind.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Student of Rav Pappa who often challenged his teachings.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: His teacher, pained by the constant objections.

terms.meaning: A posture of bowed, personal prayer said after the main prayer.
A name for God.
